title: "The itertools Crate"

# The itertools Crate

`itertools` fills gaps that do not belong in every program's standard-library vocabulary: chunking a run, sliding windows of tuples, cartesian products, combinations, and a few collectors. The traits come in through `use itertools::Itertools`.

```toml
[dependencies]
itertools = "0.14"
```

## The concept

These adaptors are still lazy, except the ones that are consumers (`join`). They allocate when the operation requires memory (`unique` remembers what it has seen, `combinations` builds each group). Prefer a `Vec` method or a short loop when it is clearer. Reach for itertools when the name of the adaptor is the name of the problem.

## Recipe 71 — Grouping consecutive elements with chunk_by()

`chunk_by` starts a new group when the key changes. It does not sort, and it does not merge equal keys that are not neighbors.

```rust
fn main() {
    use itertools::Itertools;

    let readings = [10, 10, 12, 12, 10];
    let mut runs = Vec::new();
    for (value, group) in &readings.iter().chunk_by(|n| *n) {
        runs.push((*value, group.count()));
    }
    assert_eq!(runs, [(10, 2), (12, 2), (10, 1)]);
}
```

The `for` loop borrows the `chunk_by` adaptor (`&...chunk_by`). Each group is itself an iterator, and it is only valid for that iteration. Collect or count it before the next group. The final `10` is its own run because a `12` sits between the tens.

## Recipe 72 — Sliding windows with tuple_windows()

```rust
fn main() {
    use itertools::Itertools;

    let readings = [10, 13, 12, 18];
    let jumps: Vec<(i32, i32)> = readings.into_iter().tuple_windows().collect();
    assert_eq!(jumps, [(10, 13), (13, 12), (12, 18)]);

    let rose: Vec<_> = jumps.into_iter().filter(|(a, b)| b > a).collect();
    assert_eq!(rose, [(10, 13), (12, 18)]);
}
```

`tuple_windows::<(i32, i32)>()` is inferred here. A window of three is `tuple_windows::<(i32, i32, i32)>()`. The windows overlap. This is not `chunks`, which does not overlap, and it is not `slice::windows`, which yields subslices. Tuples are the right result when the width is a small fixed number.

## Recipe 73 — Cartesian product with cartesian_product()

Every pair. The length of the output is the product of the lengths.

```rust
fn main() {
    use itertools::Itertools;

    let pairs: Vec<(i32, char)> = (1..=2).cartesian_product(['a', 'b']).collect();
    assert_eq!(pairs, [(1, 'a'), (1, 'b'), (2, 'a'), (2, 'b')]);
}
```

The right-hand iterator must be cloneable, because itertools walks it once per item on the left. A one-shot channel receiver is not a legal right-hand side. A `Vec` is.

## Recipe 74 — Combinations and permutations

Combinations ignore order and do not repeat an index. Permutations are ordered.

```rust
fn main() {
    use itertools::Itertools;

    let combos: Vec<Vec<i32>> = (1..4).combinations(2).collect();
    assert_eq!(combos, [vec![1, 2], vec![1, 3], vec![2, 3]]);

    let perms: Vec<Vec<i32>> = (1..4).permutations(2).collect();
    assert_eq!(
        perms,
        [
            vec![1, 2],
            vec![1, 3],
            vec![2, 1],
            vec![2, 3],
            vec![3, 1],
            vec![3, 2],
        ]
    );
}
```

`1..4` is `1, 2, 3`. Two-element combinations are the three unordered pairs. Permutations of length 2 include both `(1, 2)` and `(2, 1)`. Both adaptors allocate a `Vec` per group. Do not ask for combinations of a large `n` taken `k` at a time without counting the output first.

## Recipe 75 — Interleaving and merging sequences

`interleave` alternates, one item from each, until both are done. `merge` assumes each input is already sorted and produces one sorted iterator. It does not sort for you.

```rust
fn main() {
    use itertools::Itertools;

    let laced: Vec<_> = [1, 3, 5].into_iter().interleave([2, 4, 6]).collect();
    assert_eq!(laced, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]);

    let merged: Vec<_> = [1, 4, 9].into_iter().merge([2, 3, 8]).collect();
    assert_eq!(merged, [1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9]);
}
```

If the inputs of `merge` are not sorted, the output is not sorted either. Sort each side first, or collect and sort once.

## Recipe 76 — Collecting into multiple collections at once with partition_map()

`partition_map` sends each item either left or right. `Either` is how you name the side.

```rust
fn main() {
    use itertools::{Either, Itertools};

    let (hot, cold): (Vec<_>, Vec<_>) = [18, 30, 19, 41].into_iter().partition_map(|n| {
        if n >= 30 {
            Either::Left(n)
        } else {
            Either::Right(n)
        }
    });
    assert_eq!(hot, [30, 41]);
    assert_eq!(cold, [18, 19]);
}
```

`Iterator::partition` is the standard-library version when both sides have the same type and the test is a `bool`. Use `partition_map` when the two sides have different types, because each arm of `Either` can build a different value.

## Recipe 77 — Unique elements with unique() and unique_by()

`unique` remembers values it has yielded. The first occurrence wins. Later duplicates are dropped. The memory is a set of seen items, so the item type must be `Clone + Eq + Hash` for `unique`.

```rust
fn main() {
    use itertools::Itertools;

    let ids: Vec<_> = [4, 1, 4, 2, 1].into_iter().unique().collect();
    assert_eq!(ids, [4, 1, 2]);

    let words = ["ada", "bob", "linus", "grace"];
    let by_len: Vec<_> = words.into_iter().unique_by(|word| word.len()).collect();
    assert_eq!(by_len, ["ada", "linus"]);
}
```

`unique_by` remembers the key, not the whole item. `"bob"` has the same length as `"ada"`, so it is dropped. `"linus"` has a new length and stays. `"grace"` repeats that length and is dropped.

## Recipe 78 — Formatting with join() and format_with()

`join` allocates one `String`. `format_with` writes through `Display`, so it can go into `format!` or a writer without building the string twice. You still pay for the final string if you format into one.

```rust
fn main() {
    use itertools::Itertools;

    let names = ["ada", "linus", "grace"];
    assert_eq!(names.iter().join(", "), "ada, linus, grace");

    let shown = format!(
        "[{}]",
        names.iter().format_with(" | ", |name, f| f(&format_args!("{name}")))
    );
    assert_eq!(shown, "[ada | linus | grace]");
}
```

`join` needs `Display` items. References to `str` are fine. `format_with`'s closure receives the item and a formatter callback. Call the callback with something that implements `Display`.

## When to reach for itertools

Use it when the adaptor name matches the job: `unique` for first-wins dedup, `tuple_windows` for a fixed overlap, `merge` for two sorted streams, `cartesian_product` for a full grid. Skip it when `slice::windows`, `Vec::dedup`, or a three-line loop already says the same thing in the standard library. Adding the crate for one `join` is reasonable. Adding it to avoid learning `collect` is not.
